text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Despite record high unemployment and low inflation Swedish wages have risen strongly in the past years. The government is expecting employers and unions to present new rules on wage negotiations in three months to control any resulting inflationary pressures from higher wages.
- Tourism hit new levels in Stockholm in 1996 with the number of hotel and hostel nights rising to 5.7 million which was a five percent increase from 1995.

- Swedish shipping companies are in a phase of growth and optimism. Sea freight continued to grow in 1996 by 12 ships to 255 ships of which many are less than 30 years old. During the year 13 new ships were delivered for Swedish shipping companies.

- Swedish doctors said the number of casualties from drinking methanol have increased, particularly among young people. A 20-year-old man died and five others needed hospital treatment after drinking methanol at New Year celebrations.

- Computer companies were the best performers on the Stockholm bourse in 1996 which overall rose 38.3 percent with turnover of over 900 billion crowns. The biggest mover was OTC-listed IBS which rose 375 percent.
- Minors can no longer buy tobacco in Sweden under new rules to try to combat the rise in smoking amongst teenagers.

- A farmer from Lidkoping was the Bors-SM 1996 winner for choosing the best performing share portfolio. Goran Karlsson won with Taurus, Sands Petroleum, and Gambro. He invested 9,000 crowns and ended the year with 30,342 crowns, a rise of 237 percent while the market overall rose 38.3 percent.
- Four out of five Swedes think households' economy will be worse in 1997, according to a new survey by pollster Skop.
- Medical company Salus Holding is the first new company to be listed on the Stockholm bourse in 1997. Salus will be listed on the O-list from Thursday.
